earlier_scan.source_named: Franich 2014, Contour Tones and Prosodic Structure in Medumba (BLS 40); Voorhoeve 1965/1971 Bamileke phonology papers
earlier_scan.note: Grassfields tone language; prosodic-structure work exists but no stress statement loaded.

new_statements.quote: In this paper, I have shown that a single type of metrical foot structure is useful for characterizing both segmental and tonal processes in Medʉmba, a Grassfields Bantu language. Furthermore, I have shown that, despite the lack of stress in Medʉmba, heads of trochaic feet in the language display temporal properties consistent with metrical prominence found in stress-based languages such as English.
new_statements.citation: Franich, Kathryn. 2018. Evidence for metrical prominence asymmetries in Medʉmba. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 5 (AMP 2017, New York). Washington, DC: Linguistic Society of America. doi:10.3765/amp.v5i0.4259
new_statements.locator: §6 Conclusion, p. 11 (supporting statements: p. 2 §2; p. 5 (10); Franich 2014 BLS 40 p. 110; Franich 2017 diss. p. xiii and p. 90)
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (12 pp., XeTeX text layer, no scanned needed). The quoted passage is on p.11 under "6 Conclusion" exactly as given: "In this paper, I have shown that a single type of metrical foot structure is useful for characterizing both segmental and tonal processes in Medʉmba, a Grassfields Bantu language. Furthermore, I have shown that, despite the lack of stress in Medʉmba, heads of trochaic feet in the language display temporal properties consistent with metrical prominence found in stress-based languages such as English." (extracted text renders the ʉ glyph as "0"; otherwise word-for-word). Surrounding section read: §1 (p.1) frames African tone languages as "typically lack[ing] stress"; §2…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Medʉmba is a two-tone (H/L) language with no word stress. It does have word-level metrical prominence: stems are parsed into maximally disyllabic trochaic feet built from right to left and right-aligned with the prosodic word, so the foot head is the stem-initial syllable (the penult of a disyllabic stem, the first syllable of a monosyllabic one). Diagnostics: only the stem-initial syllable carries the full 48-consonant/11-vowel inventory (non-initial syllables have 7 consonants and only [ə]); stem-medial consonants lenite; falling contour tones are allowed only in foot-head position; in trisyllabic English loans a H tone is placed on the penult even where the source has no stress there; in speech-cycling experiments stem-initial syllables (not prefixes or stem-final syllables) align to harmonic phase positions like English stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable (no stress). Franich 2021 (preprint p.32) notes that Medʉmba lacks 'hallmarks of a stress system, such as... evidence for cyclic secondary stress' as a general point about such languages; feet are maximally disyllabic and multiple feet can be parsed in longer (loan) words, e.g. ká(bí.ndə̀) 'carpenter' (Franich 2014 p.112).
new_statements.exceptions: Pronominal enclitics behave like foot heads in speech cycling despite showing clitic-like lenition (Franich 2018 p.10; 2017 p.90-91; 2021 §5.1) — treated as a change in progress. Compounds are excluded from the foot generalizations (Franich 2014 fn.5). Echo vowels after glottal consonants in some verb roots are an apparent exception to V2 = schwa (Franich 2014 fn.5).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level: prominence is defined on the prosodic word (stem plus affixes), with the foot head at the stem-initial syllable; elicited words and repeated short sentences (speech-cycling experiments, speakers from Bangangté/Bazou/Bangoulap). A separate phrase-level high preverbal phrase accent is described in Franich 2019/2021 Language and Speech. Speakers are from the Bangangté area (Bazou and Bangoulap dialects mentioned).
new_statements.identity_note: All Franich sources describe Medʉmba (Bamileke-Medumba, ISO byv, Glottolog medu1238) as spoken around Bangangté, Ndé division, Cameroon, with speakers from the Bazou and Bangoulap dialects noted; Voorhoeve's older work is labelled 'Bamileke (Bangangté dialect)', which is the same variety. No differently named variety is involved.

sources.locator: §6 Conclusion, p. 11 (supporting statements: p. 2 §2; p. 5 (10); Franich 2014 BLS 40 p. 110; Franich 2017 diss. p. xiii and p. 90)
sources.note: States outright that Medʉmba lacks stress (p.11) but has trochaic feet whose heads (stem-initial syllables) show metrical prominence; contour tones and full segmental contrasts are restricted to foot heads (pp.3-5).

sources.citation: Franich, Kathryn. 2021 [online 2019]. Uncovering tonal and temporal correlates of phrasal prominence in Medʉmba. Language and Speech 64(4). doi:10.1177/0023830919887994 (author preprint, 51 pp.)
sources.note: Phrase-level: a high preverbal phrase accent sensitive to prosodic boundaries and metrical prominence; defines 'stress' as phonetically measurable word-level prominence and does not attribute it to Medʉmba; reviews initial/penultimate prominence in Bantu generally.

sources.citation: Franich, Kathryn. 2021. Metrical prominence asymmetries in Medʉmba, a Grassfields Bantu language. Language 97(2): 365-402. doi:10.1353/lan.2021.0021 (author preprint revised 2020-12-17, 74 pp.)
sources.note: Preprint p.5: Medʉmba 'does not meet all of the typical phonetic criteria for a metrically based stress system. In the case of Medʉmba, stem-initial syllables appear to show evidence of greater prominence'; p.6-7: 48 consonants/11 vowels stem-initially vs 7 consonants/only [ə] non-initially; stems maximally disyllabic feet with contrasts at left edge; p.32: 'at least some African tone languages have genuine metrical prominence asymmetries at the word level'. Published version paywalled (Project MUSE).

sources.citation: Franich, Kathryn. 2017. The Interaction of Prominence, Rhythm, and Tone in Medʉmba. PhD dissertation, University of Chicago, 210 pp.
sources.note: Abstract p.xiii: Medʉmba is 'a Grassfields Bantu language with a robust system of lexical tone but which displays little phonetic evidence of stress or accent'; stem-initial syllables show greater prominence than stem-final and non-stem syllables. Ch.5 (pp.47-91): trochaic foot right-aligned with the prosodic word so the foot head is the stem-initial syllable (p.90); pronominal enclitics unexpectedly also prominent.

sources.citation: Franich, Kathryn H. 2014. Contour tones and prosodic structure in Medʉmba. Proceedings of the 40th Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society, 102-124. doi:10.3765/bls.v40i0.3135
sources.note: p.110: foot structure 'has not been described in previous work on the Grassfields languages'; 'Medʉmba builds trochaic feet which are optimally disyllabic and which are built from right to left' (evidence: V2 of roots is always schwa; H tone lands on the penult of trisyllabic English loans). No stress claimed; tone language.

sources.citation: Keupdjio, Hermann Sidoine. 2020. The syntax of A'-dependencies in Bamileke Medumba. PhD dissertation, University of British Columbia, 406 pp. (Glottolog ref 680289; lingbuzz/005521)
sources.note: Syntax dissertation; §3.1.1 (pp.108-110) reviews competing tone inventories (2-tone Voorhoeve 1974/Franich 2014; 4-tone Wandji 1993; 5-tone Tondji 1979/Kouankem 2012) and pp.9-10 survey the descriptive literature; nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: Franich, Kathryn. 2018. Tonal and morphophonological effects on the location of perceptual centers (p-centers): Evidence from a Bantu language. Journal of Phonetics 67: 21-33 (author preprint)
sources.note: Tone (two-level H/L) and prenasalization only; silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Danis, Nick, Jonathan Barnes & Catherine O'Connor. 2012. Downstep and contour formation in Medumba: A prosodic account. Selected Proceedings of the 42nd Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 23-31. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla.
sources.note: Phonological-word and clitic boundaries diagnosed by Voorhoeve's (1965) consonant alternations (lateralization, spirantization, final devoicing) and downstep; no mention of stress or accent.
